title: Sequences
explanation: A sequence runs instructions in order. Changing that order can change what happens.
example: Move right twice, then down once. What changes if you reverse the order?

title: Variables
explanation: A variable is a named place to store a value. Your robot's energy is a variable.
example: Start energy at 5. Add 3. Is energy now at least 8?

title: AND
explanation: AND is true only when both conditions are true.
example: Test a key with low energy, then a key with energy 8. Which opens an AND gate?

title: OR
explanation: OR is true when at least one condition is true. Both can also be true.
example: Try a key with no energy, then no key with energy 8.

title: NOT
explanation: NOT reverses a Boolean value. True becomes false; false becomes true.
example: If has key is false, what is NOT has key?

title: Binary truth values
explanation: A bit is 0 or 1. In our logic puzzles, 1 represents true and 0 represents false.
example: Write 1 for an open gate and 0 for a closed gate.

title: If / else
explanation: IF runs one branch when a condition is true. ELSE runs the alternative when it is false.
example: If energy is at least 8, open the gate; else show a hint.

title: Switch / case
explanation: Switch chooses an action by matching a value to a named case. A default handles unmatched values.
example: For a signal: red means stop, green means go, and default means wait.

title: Loops
explanation: A loop repeats instructions. A counted repeat runs a known number of times.
example: Repeat move right 3 times. How many movement blocks does that replace?

title: While
explanation: WHILE checks a condition before each turn. It can run zero times if the condition starts false.
example: While energy is below 8, collect energy. What must change to make it stop?

title: Do / while
explanation: DO / WHILE performs its action once before checking the condition, so it always runs at least once.
example: Take one step, then check whether another step is safe.

title: Functions
explanation: A function gives a reusable group of instructions a name.
example: Name a right-then-down sequence cross corner. Where could you use it twice?

title: Debugging
explanation: Debugging means finding why a program behaves unexpectedly and testing a change.
example: Predict the next square, run one instruction, and compare what happened.

title: Prompting
explanation: A clear prompt includes a goal, useful context, constraints and a response format. Check the answer rather than assuming it is right.
example: Ask for two hints about a gate, without giving the solution or sharing personal details.
